title: Radio Transmitters: Gimbals, Switches & EdgeTX
html:
The radio is your most permanent investment

Frames, motors, and props are consumables. A good radio outlives a dozen quads, so buy once and buy well. The dominant ecosystem today is EdgeTX firmware (the successor to OpenTX) running on radios like the RadioMaster Boxer, RadioMaster TX16S, Jumper T-Pro, and TBS Tango 2. Many ship with a built-in ELRS module, which is the recommendation for new pilots.

Anatomy of the transmitter

  • Gimbals — the two spring-loaded sticks. Each gimbal moves on two axes, giving four primary control channels. Quality matters: Hall-effect gimbals (magnetic, contactless) outlast cheap potentiometer gimbals and never develop center drift.
  • Mode 2 — the near-universal stick layout: left stick = Throttle (vertical) + Yaw (horizontal), right stick = Pitch (vertical) + Roll (horizontal). Learn Mode 2 unless you have a strong reason not to.
  • Switches — 2-position (SA...), 3-position, and momentary switches used for arming, mode changes, beeper, and turtle mode.
  • Trims, pots, and sliders — analog or stepped inputs. On a quad you rarely use trims; an acro quad should fly with all trims centered.
  • Bay / internal module — where the RF module lives. JR-bay radios accept external modules; many modern radios have ELRS baked in.

Throttle: self-centering vs ratcheted

For multirotor you want a non-self-centering throttle with a smooth (frictioned) or ratcheted detent so the stick stays where you put it. Radios like the Boxer let you swap the gimbal tension mechanically. A self-centering throttle is for planes, not quads.

Navigating EdgeTX

EdgeTX organizes everything into a Model (per-aircraft config) and Radio Settings (global). Key screens reached from the main view: Model Select, Model Setup, Inputs, Mixes, Outputs, Logical Switches, Special Functions, and the Channel Monitor. The wheel/roller plus ENT and RTN buttons drive navigation; long-press ENT opens context menus.

EdgeTX — Channel Monitor
CH1 Ail +0.0% CH2 Ele +0.0% CH3 Thr -100% (throttle low = safe) CH4 Rud +0.0% CH5 SA -100% (disarmed)
Naming saves grief.
Name each model after the quad (frame + size), not Model01. When you own five quads you will thank yourself, and you avoid arming the wrong model with the wrong failsafe.
Props off for all bench work.
Any time you bind, test channels, or arm at a desk, remove the propellers. A quad that spins up unexpectedly with props on causes lacerations.
▸Hands-On

Create a new model and confirm every input moves.

  1. From the main screen open Model Select and create a new model named after your build.
  2. Set the model to Multirotor; verify the throttle source is the correct stick.
  3. Open the Channel Monitor (long-press the page button or use the telemetry/monitor screen).
  4. Move each gimbal axis and confirm CH1-CH4 respond and return to center (except throttle).
  5. Flick each switch and watch its channel jump between -100%, 0%, and +100%.

title: Control Link Protocols: ELRS vs Crossfire/TBS
html:
What the control link does

The control link is the radio path carrying your stick commands to the flight controller and (optionally) telemetry back. It is separate from the video link. Two systems dominate: ExpressLRS (ELRS) — open source — and TBS Crossfire / Tracer from Team BlackSheep. Both are long-range systems that left the old 2.4GHz toy protocols far behind.

ExpressLRS

ELRS is open source, cheap, and extremely capable. It runs on 2.4GHz or 900MHz hardware. Its headline feature is selectable packet rates: from 50Hz (maximum range, higher latency) up to 500Hz and even 1000Hz on 2.4GHz (lowest latency, shortest range). Higher packet rate means lower latency but less link budget. A typical freestyle pilot runs 250Hz or 500Hz; a long-range pilot drops to 50Hz or 100Hz.

TBS Crossfire / Tracer

Crossfire runs on 900MHz and is legendary for raw long range and reliability; Tracer is the 2.4GHz, lower-latency sibling. Crossfire is a polished, closed commercial product with excellent build quality and strong support, at higher cost. Crossfire's fixed packet-rate options are coarser than ELRS, and latency on 900MHz Crossfire is higher than 2.4GHz ELRS at high rates.

Frequency tradeoffs

900MHz penetrates obstacles and trees better and reaches farther for a given power; antennas are larger. 2.4GHz allows higher packet rates (lower latency) and smaller antennas but is more line-of-sight dependent and shares spectrum with WiFi and some video.

AttributeELRS 2.4GHzELRS 900MHzCrossfire 900MHz
Min latency~2-5ms (500-1000Hz)~10-20ms~13-30ms
Packet rates50/150/250/500/1000Hz25/50/100/200Hz50/150Hz
RangeVery longExtremeExtreme
RX cost~$8-20~$15-25~$30-50
EcosystemOpen sourceOpen sourceClosed / TBS
Match TX power to need.
ELRS lets you set TX output (25mW, 100mW, 250mW, 1W and up). More power means more range but more battery drain and heat, and power limits are regulated. Most line-of-sight flying needs only 25-100mW.
Power and frequency are regulated.
Legal RF power and which bands you may use vary by country. 900MHz allocations differ between the US (902-928MHz ISM) and the EU (868MHz). Verify your current local limits before raising TX power.
▸Hands-On

Build a comparison sheet and choose a link.

  1. Make a table with columns: frequency, packet/RF rates, typical latency, claimed range, RX price.
  2. Fill rows for ELRS 2.4GHz, ELRS 900MHz, and Crossfire.
  3. Note your flying style (freestyle line-of-sight, racing, or long range).
  4. Pick one link and write two sentences justifying it on latency, range, and cost.

title: Binding Your Radio to the Receiver
html:
What binding actually does

Binding pairs one transmitter module to one receiver so they share a unique identity and will not respond to anyone else's radio. With ELRS, the pairing is established by a shared binding phrase rather than a button dance: set the same phrase on TX and RX and they bind automatically on power-up. Crossfire uses a traditional bind button / bind menu.

ELRS binding by phrase (recommended)

ELRS firmware lets you flash both the TX module and the RX with the same binding phrase (a short text string). When both carry the same phrase, they auto-bind every time. This eliminates the timing-sensitive button procedure and means a replacement RX just needs the same phrase flashed.

  1. Flash your TX module and RX to the same ELRS major version (for example both 3.x). Mismatched major versions will not bind.
  2. Set an identical binding phrase on both during the flash, or via the ExpressLRS Lua / Web UI.
  3. Power the quad; the RX LED goes from fast blink (searching) to solid (linked).

Manual ELRS bind (no phrase)

  1. Power the RX. Power-cycle it 3 times quickly; on the 3rd boot it enters bind mode (slow double-blink).
  2. On the radio open the ExpressLRS Lua script (Model Setup then Tools, or the SYS/Tools menu) and select Bind.
  3. The RX LED goes solid when bound.

Confirming a stable link

Open the ELRS Lua script and check the live stats, then verify telemetry on the radio. Two key numbers:

  • LQ (Link Quality) — percent of packets received. Should sit at 100 at rest. LQ dropping is the real warning sign in flight, more than RSSI.
  • RSSI (dBm) — signal strength. Closer to 0 is stronger (for example -40dBm next to the bench). The link fades out near the receiver's sensitivity floor (often around -105 to -112dBm depending on packet rate).
ExpressLRS Lua — link stats at rest
Pkt Rate 250Hz TLM Ratio 1:64 Power 100mW LQ 100 RSSI -42dBm (bench, very strong) Link CONNECTED
Props off, throttle low.
Always bind and test with propellers removed and the throttle stick all the way down. Set up failsafe (next lesson) before you ever fly.
Version mismatch is the #1 bind failure.
If a bind will not take, check that TX and RX run the same ELRS major version. Re-flash one to match the other.
▸Hands-On

Bind the link and record link health.

  1. Confirm props are off and throttle is down.
  2. Bind via matching phrase (or manual 3x power-cycle plus Lua Bind).
  3. Confirm the RX LED is solid and CH1-CH4 move in the Channel Monitor.
  4. Open the ELRS Lua stats and record LQ and RSSI at rest.

title: Channels, Mixes & Switch Assignments
html:
From sticks to channels

The radio sends a numbered list of channel values to the flight controller. CH1-CH4 are almost always the four flight axes (in Betaflight's default AETR mapping: Aileron/Roll, Elevator/Pitch, Throttle, Rudder/Yaw). CH5 and up are aux channels driven by switches, used for arming and mode selection.

The EdgeTX signal chain

Three stages process each control: Inputs (raw stick/switch with optional expo and weight) then Mixes (combine sources into a channel) then Outputs (final scaling, limits, and reverse). For a quad you mostly assign switches directly to channels in the Mixes page.

Standard aux assignments

ChannelSwitchFunction
CH5 / AUX1SA (2-pos)Arm
CH6 / AUX2SB (3-pos)Flight mode (Angle/Horizon/Acro)
CH7 / AUX3SC (momentary)Beeper / find-quad
CH8 / AUX4SD (2-pos)Turtle (flip-over-after-crash)

Why a 3-position switch for modes

A 3-position switch gives three values (-100% / 0% / +100%), so a single switch covers three flight modes. In Betaflight's Modes tab you set ranges: for example ANGLE active 1000-1300us, HORIZON 1300-1700us, and the top position (1700-2000us) leaving Acro (no self-leveling mode active = rate/acro).

Microseconds, not percent

Betaflight reads aux channels in microseconds (us), roughly 1000-2000us. EdgeTX shows -100% to +100%. The mapping is: -100% = ~1000us, 0% = ~1500us, +100% = ~2000us. When you set mode ranges in Betaflight, flick the switch and watch the yellow marker to place ranges exactly under each position.

EdgeTX Mixes — aux switch map
CH05 SA Weight 100 (Arm) CH06 SB Weight 100 (Modes 3-pos) CH07 SC Weight 100 (Beeper) CH08 SD Weight 100 (Turtle)
Keep mixes simple.
You can build a logical-switch mix so one slider plays a voice alert or triggers the beeper on a momentary press. Start simple: one switch, one channel, one function. Complexity is where mistakes hide.
Arm switch placement matters.
Put arm on a switch you cannot bump accidentally, and never assign arm to a momentary or a switch shared with another function. Confirm the quad disarms the instant you flip arm off.
▸Hands-On

Assign four switches and document the map.

  1. In EdgeTX Mixes, map SA to CH5 (arm), SB to CH6 (modes), SC to CH7 (beeper), SD to CH8 (turtle).
  2. Open the Channel Monitor and confirm each channel jumps as you flick its switch.
  3. In Betaflight's Modes tab, set the ranges by flicking each switch and watching the marker.
  4. Write down your channel map (channel, switch, function, us values) and keep it with the model.

title: Failsafe: The Most Important Safety Setting
html:
Why failsafe is non-negotiable

Radio links fail. You will fly behind a building, out of range, or hit interference, and the quad will lose signal. Failsafe defines what the quad does when that happens. A quad with no verified failsafe is a flying weapon: if it holds the last throttle command it can fly away at full speed into people or property. Configuring and testing failsafe is the single most important safety task before flight.

The two-layer system

Failsafe has two cooperating layers and both must be correct:

  1. Receiver failsafe — what the RX outputs when it loses the TX. On ELRS, set the RX to No Pulses (the RX stops sending channel data) rather than holding last values. When the FC sees no valid signal, its own failsafe takes over cleanly.
  2. Flight controller failsafe (Betaflight Failsafe tab) — what the FC does when it loses valid RX data. The default and correct stage-2 procedure for line-of-sight is Drop (cut motors immediately). This makes the quad fall straight down instead of flying away.

Drop vs Land vs GPS Rescue

For freestyle/racing line-of-sight, Drop is safest: the quad stops where contact is lost. Land (auto-descend) and GPS Rescue (fly home and land) are for long-range quads with a GPS module and a tuned rescue procedure. Never enable GPS Rescue without configuring and field-testing it; a bad rescue config can fly the quad away.

Betaflight CLI — verify failsafe
get failsafe_procedure failsafe_procedure = DROP get failsafe_delay failsafe_delay = 4 (0.4s guard time) RX set: ELRS failsafe = No Pulses save

How to test it (the part people skip)

Configuring failsafe is not enough; you must verify it. With props removed, arm the quad on the bench, then turn off the radio. The motors must stop within a fraction of a second and the FC OSD should show FAILSAFE. If the motors keep spinning or the quad disarms slowly, your settings are wrong. Re-check RX failsafe = No Pulses and FC procedure = Drop.

SAFETY: never fly without verified failsafe.
Test on every quad, and re-test after any firmware update or receiver change. Always test with propellers OFF. Treat an untested quad as unflyable.
Set the warning beeper.
Configure a low-RSSI / low-LQ OSD warning and a lost-model audible alarm so you get a cue before the link fully drops, giving you time to turn back.
▸Hands-On

Set failsafe to drop and prove it works.

  1. Set ELRS RX failsafe to No Pulses.
  2. In Betaflight Failsafe tab set procedure to Drop; save.
  3. Remove all propellers. Arm the quad on a stable surface at low throttle.
  4. Power off the radio and confirm motors cut instantly and OSD shows FAILSAFE.
  5. Log the result (pass/fail) and the disarm time in your build notes.

title: Flight Modes: Acro vs Angle vs Horizon
html:
Self-leveling vs rate control

The flight controller can interpret your stick inputs two fundamentally different ways. Understanding the difference shapes your entire learning path.

Angle mode (self-leveling)

Stick position commands an angle. Push the right stick halfway forward and the quad tilts to a fixed angle; release it and the quad returns to level by itself. There is a maximum lean angle, so you cannot flip or roll. This is the most forgiving mode and how most camera drones (DJI) behave by default. Great for first hovers and orientation practice.

Horizon mode (hybrid)

Like Angle near center (self-levels when you release the sticks), but if you push the stick fully to the stop it allows full rotations (flips and rolls). It is a bridge, but it has quirks: the transition between leveling and rate can feel unpredictable, and it teaches habits you must unlearn. Many instructors skip it.

Acro / Rate mode (no self-leveling)

Stick position commands a rotation rate, not an angle. Center stick means hold current attitude; the quad does not self-level. If you tilt forward and center the stick, it stays tilted and accelerates. This is what every freestyle and racing pilot flies, because it gives full 3D control: flips, rolls, dives, inverted flight. It is harder to learn but is the real skill ceiling.

ModeSelf-levels?Can flip/roll?Best for
AngleYesNoFirst hovers, orientation
HorizonCenter onlyAt full stickOptional bridge
AcroNoYesFreestyle, racing, all real FPV
Acro is the destination.
Angle is training wheels. Spend most of your early time in a simulator in Acro so you build the muscle memory you actually need; use Angle on a real quad only for your very first line-of-sight hovers if at all.
Mode switching in flight.
Set your 3-position switch deliberately and know which position is which before you arm. Accidentally dropping into Acro at low altitude with no rate skills will crash the quad. Practice mode awareness on the bench (props off) first.
▸Hands-On

Write a one-page learning-mode plan.

  1. State which mode you will fly first and on what platform (sim vs real).
  2. Define your sim goal in Acro: stable hover, then figure-8s, then dives.
  3. List concrete graduation criteria (for example: 5 hours sim in Acro, consistent hover within 1m, recover from inverted).
  4. Note when (if ever) you will use Angle on the real quad and why.

title: The FPV Video Link: Analog vs Digital, Goggles & Antennas
html:
Seeing through the drone

The video link is entirely separate from the control link. A camera on the quad feeds a video transmitter (VTX) that broadcasts on (typically) 5.8GHz to your goggles. Two worlds exist: analog and digital.

Analog (5.8GHz)

The classic FPV standard. Lowest latency (often under 30ms), cheapest, and it degrades gracefully — as signal weakens you get static and noise but usually still a usable picture, so you can fly out and feel the edge of range. Resolution is low and the image is noisy, but for racing and learning it is rock solid. VTX power is selectable (25/200/600mW and up) on bands like Raceband; channel coordination matters when flying with others.

Digital (HD)

Systems like DJI O3/O4, Walksnail Avatar, and open-source HDZero deliver a sharp, high-resolution image. DJI and Walksnail are higher latency but stunning clarity; HDZero is lower latency and degrades more gracefully (more analog-like). The tradeoff: digital tends to hold a perfect image then break up abruptly ("cliff edge") at the range limit rather than fading, and gear is pricier and heavier.

Goggles vs box/screen

Goggles (two small screens with lenses) give true immersion and are what most pilots use. Box goggles (single screen) and standalone monitors/screens are cheaper and great for a spotter or for getting started, but lack the immersion and head-tracking feel.

Antennas: omni vs directional

  • Omnidirectional (for example a circular-polarized "pagoda" or lollipop) radiates roughly equally in all horizontal directions. Best for close-in freestyle and proximity flying where the quad is all around you.
  • Directional (patch, helical, Crosshair) focuses gain in one direction for much greater range, but you must keep the quad roughly in front of you. Best for long range and racing down a straight.
  • Diversity receivers use both at once and automatically select the stronger feed per moment. The standard pro setup: one omni for all-around coverage plus one patch for distance.
SAFETY: spotter and visual-line-of-sight.
Wearing goggles blinds you to the real world. Fly with a spotter who keeps eyes on the aircraft and airspace, can warn you of people or hazards, and helps you maintain visual line of sight. Many jurisdictions legally require a visual observer for FPV.
Verify VTX power and FPV rules.
Legal 5.8GHz VTX output power and goggle/FPV operating rules vary by country and may require a license (for example an amateur-radio license for higher power). Confirm current FAA / local regulations before transmitting.
▸Hands-On

Spec a complete video system.

  1. Choose a system type (analog, DJI/Walksnail digital, or HDZero) and justify it for your flying style.
  2. Pick goggles or a screen and note resolution/latency.
  3. Select two antenna types for a diversity setup (one omni, one directional).
  4. Explain in two sentences why that antenna pairing fits how you intend to fly.

title: Learning Safely in a Simulator
html:
The cheapest, safest way to learn

Every crash on a real quad costs money, time, and possibly a body part. A simulator costs nothing per crash and lets you fly hundreds of times in an afternoon. The single biggest predictor of how fast a new pilot becomes competent is sim hours logged in Acro. Treat the sim as your primary training tool for the first many hours.

Why your real radio, not a gamepad

Plug your actual transmitter into the sim so the muscle memory you build transfers directly to the field. Most EdgeTX radios connect over USB and present as a USB joystick / game controller (HID mode). Some sims also support connecting via the radio's trainer port or via a dedicated dongle. Use the same stick mode (Mode 2) and similar rates to your real quad.

Popular simulators

  • Liftoff — polished, large community, good for freestyle and racing.
  • Velocidrone — the racer's choice; precise physics, great for gates and tracks.
  • Uncrashed and DRL Simulator — accessible and fun; DRL is free and excellent for beginners.
  • FPV.SkyDive / Tryp — additional options worth trying.

Connecting the radio

  1. On the radio, set the USB mode to USB Joystick (HID) when you plug in (EdgeTX prompts you, or set it under SYS / Hardware).
  2. In the sim's controller settings, calibrate: move every stick to its extremes so the sim maps the axes.
  3. Map throttle, yaw, pitch, roll and confirm none are reversed; set arm to a switch as on the real quad.
EdgeTX — USB connect prompt
USB connected. Select mode: USB Storage (SD card) > USB Joystick (HID) <-- choose this for sims USB Serial (VCP)

What to practice first

In Acro mode: a stable hover, then small forward flights, then yaw spins while keeping position (orientation training), then figure-8s, then gentle dives. Orientation — knowing which way is forward when the quad faces you — is the hardest early skill. Drill it deliberately.

Short, frequent, deliberate.
Three 20-minute focused sessions beat one exhausted 3-hour grind. Pick one skill per session and repeat it until it is boring, then move on.
Bench-test the real quad too.
The sim cannot replace verifying failsafe and arming behavior on the physical quad. Before your first real flight, confirm failsafe (Lesson 4.5) with props off.
▸Hands-On

Connect your radio and log your first 30 minutes.

  1. Plug the radio in via USB and select USB Joystick (HID).
  2. Calibrate all four axes in the sim and confirm none are reversed.
  3. Fly 30 minutes of hover and yaw-orientation practice in Acro.
  4. Write notes: what felt hardest (likely orientation), and one skill to drill next session.
